As of 500 AM Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Waves of showers and thunderstorms with excessive 
rain will focus along a slow-moving, outflow-reinforced/strengthened 
cold front through Thu-Thu night.

Within a trough anchored by a mid/upr-level cyclone that will lift 
through QC, a compact shortwave perturbation evident over wrn ON in 
GOES-E water vapor satellite data will dig sewd into the lwr Great 
Lakes through this evening, then probably phase with the lifting 
cyclone across QC through Thu. The digging wave will maintain 
generally neutral to weakly rising height tendencies throughout the 
Middle Atlantic today, followed by more-strongly rising heights 
within a weakening ern CONUS trough Thu-Thu night. Cntl NC will 
remain situated within the base of that trough and probably 
influenced most strongly by MCVs of varying size and strength that 
will both progress newd from the TN Valley and srn Appalachians this 
morning and also develop in situ from regenerative convection over 
the srn Middle Atlantic, and also within a deeply moist swly flow 
regime characterized by PWs of 2-2.5" and up to 125% or so of 
normal; weakly veering winds from the surface through the mid-levels 
(indicative of WAA and contribution to QG forcing for ascent); and 
uniformly 30-40 kt wind speeds in the 850-500 mb layer. Related 
small upwind propagation/Corfidi vectors will favor training and 
backbuilding convection along and into a similarly-aligned low-level 
frontal zone that will strengthen and settle very slowly ssewd 
across the srn Middle Atlantic. 

That low-level frontal zone will tend to consolidate and strengthen, 
as a couple of closely-spaced synoptic fronts now stretching from 
the Middle Atlantic to the lwr OH Valley merge and probably 
ultimately overtake an outflow-reinforced/effective one stretching 
from the srn Delmarva and srn VA to the Cumberland Mountains. That 
effective front will continue to settle very slowly ssewd and into 
the nrn Piedmont and nrn Coastal Plain of NC through early tonight, 
while strengthening from repeated rounds of convection and diabatic 
cooling along it and differential diabatic heating today across it. 
Strengthening frontogenesis, and also isentropic lift induced by a 
30-35 kt swly low-level jet and WAA intersecting the slowly-ssewd 
settling front, will favor focused lift in the aforementioned deeply 
moist environment. When combined with broader low/mid-level WAA 
regime and influence from MCVs, amid deeply moist and conditionally 
unstable profiles, the environment will be very highly conducive for 
repeated rounds of training convection and risk of flash flooding 
initially across the nrn Piedmont and nrn Coastal Plain. This risk 
will be greatest tonight, when the boundary will probably be slowest-
moving and nearly stationary and also centered most-squarely over 
the nrn Piedmont and nrn Coastal Plain, including over the urban 
areas of the Greater Triad and Triangle. As the boundary likely gets 
overtaken by the upstream, synoptic fronts, it will probably 
accelerate and progress sewd and across the Sandhills, srn Piedmont, 
and cntl and srn Coastal Plain on Thu, where the flash flood risk 
has the potential to be somewhat less than the adjacent Piedmont and 
nrn Coastal Plain given a shorter residence time of the strongest 
frontal forcing. 

While a few strong to severe downbursts will also be possible, the 
latest SWODY1 has mostly a Marginal (Level 1 of 5) risk over cntl 
NC; and the flash flood risk will be relatively greater and the main 
story.

It will otherwise trend markedly milder behind the front Thu into 
Fri, when record low maximum temperatures have a very realistic 
chance of being set. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... The slow moving cold front across the Carolinas 
will settle south and stall across the southern Carolinas for Friday 
and into the weekend with the area of widespread rain shifting south 
and the rainfall intensity decreasing on Friday and especially 
Saturday.  

The multi-day rain event across the Carolinas will begin to shift 
south and east on Friday and begin to transition away from deep 
convection and excessive rain on Friday night. As the front settles 
further south on Friday and dewpoints in the lower 60s filter into 
the Piedmont, low level instability will decrease across northern 
portions of the Piedmont on Friday with some residual instability 
persisting across the Sandhills and southern Coastal Plain. Thus the 
precipitation across the north should have fewer thunderstorms with 
high precipitation rates and more showers or areas of lighter rain 
on Friday as isentropic lift drives more of the precipitation. To 
the south and southeast, dew points will range in the upper 60s and 
the instability will linger supporting additional thunderstorms on 
Friday and possibly Friday night. With the decreased instability and 
lighter flow aloft, the severe storm risk is greatly reduced and
